note: Came into Italian through English sailors' 'chin-chin', itself from Chinese 'qǐng qǐng' (please, please). Also 'Salute!' when clinking glasses.
Reciprocal form of 'vedere'. Add a time: 'ci vediamo domani', 'ci vediamo alle otto'. Casual but fine with almost anyone.
Used from mid-afternoon onwards, both on arriving and on leaving. 'Buon pomeriggio' (good afternoon) exists but is rarely said.
Only when parting for the night or going to bed, never as a greeting on arrival.
The everyday 'OK', used to agree, to check ('va bene?') and to close a deal. 'Ok' itself is also very common in Italy.
Latin 'salve', imperative of 'salvere' (to be in good health). A safe middle ground when 'ciao' feels too familiar and 'buongiorno' too stiff.
Stronger than plain 'grazie'; 'mille grazie' and 'grazie tante' also exist, but 'grazie tante' can sound sarcastic.
Imperative of 'figurarsi'. An informal 'you're welcome' or 'no problem'; the formal version is 'si figuri'. It can also mean 'no way!'.

example.en: Thanks for the help! – Don't mention it!

note: 'Per piacere' and 'per cortesia' are equally common; 'per cortesia' sounds slightly more formal.
Imperative of 'scusare' (Latin excusare). With people you address as 'Lei' use 'scusi' or 'mi scusi'.
The 'Lei' form: used to get a stranger's attention or to apologise to someone you do not know.
Expresses regret or sympathy ('dispiacere' = to displease). Not used to get attention; for that use 'scusi' or 'permesso'.

en: Excuse me (to get past) / may I come in?
note: Past participle of 'permettere'. Said when squeezing through a crowd and, as a question, when stepping into someone's home.
Uses 'stare' (Latin stare, to stand), not 'essere'. The formal version is 'Come sta?'.
Very common and works at any level of formality. Typical answers: 'bene', 'tutto bene', 'non c'è male' (not bad).
Built on 'grazia' with the prefix 'rin-'. Takes a direct object: 'ti ringrazio' (I thank you). Past participle 'ringraziato'.

example.en: I thank you from the heart.

note: From Latin 'placere' (to please). Also the noun 'pleasure' and the verb 'to please / to like'. Fuller form: 'Piacere di conoscerti' (informal) / 'conoscerLa' (formal).
'Bene' + 'venuto' (past participle of venire), exactly like English 'wel-come'. Agrees with the person: benvenuta, benvenuti, benvenute.
'Presto' means soon or quickly; English borrowed it as a musical tempo and a magician's word.
Same pattern as 'a presto', 'a domani' (see you tomorrow), 'a stasera' (see you tonight).
'Giornata' with the suffix '-ata' means the day as a span of time, so it wishes a good day ahead; 'buongiorno' is only the greeting. Same pair: 'sera' / 'buona serata'.
The plain wish. Many Italians prefer 'in bocca al lupo' (into the wolf's mouth), to which the answer is 'crepi!' (may it die), never 'grazie'.

en: please do / I'm counting on you
note: A hard-to-translate plea added to requests and advice, much loved by Italian parents: 'Mi raccomando, chiamami!' (Do call me, please!).
Plural of 'augurio', from Latin 'augurium' (omen). 'Tanti auguri' is the standard happy-birthday wish; also used at Christmas and New Year.
Said for achievements (an exam, a promotion, a baby). English 'compliment' reached it through French from Italian 'complimento'.
English took 'zero' from Italian, which had it from Medieval Latin 'zephirum', from Arabic 'ṣifr' (also the source of 'cipher').
Also the indefinite article: 'un', 'uno' (before s+consonant, z), 'una', 'un''. In counting the full form 'uno' is used.
Latin 'duo'. Pronounced 'DOO-eh', two syllables.
Latin 'tres'. Takes a written accent in compounds: 'ventitré', 'trentatré'.
Latin 'quattuor'. Note the double 't', pronounced long. 'Pizza quattro stagioni' = four seasons pizza.
Latin 'quinque'. 'C' before 'i' sounds like English 'ch': 'CHEEN-kweh'.
Identical in spelling to 'sei' = 'you are' (from essere); context tells them apart.
Latin 'septem'; the 'pt' cluster became a double 't', a regular Italian change (also 'scritto', 'otto').
Latin 'octo'; 'ct' became 'tt'. Before 'otto' the tens drop their final vowel: 'ventotto', 'trentotto'.
Latin 'novem'. Do not confuse with 'nuovo' (new), which has a diphthong.
Latin 'decem'. 'C' before 'i' = 'ch': 'DYEH-chee'. Appears as '-dici' in 11–16 and 'dici-' in 17–19.
'Un' + '-dici' (ten): the unit comes first in 11–16, the opposite of 17–19.
'Do' (from due) + '-dici'. Stress is on the first syllable: 'DOH-dee-chee'.
'Tre' + '-dici', stress on 'tre'. In Italy 13 is traditionally lucky; 17 is the unlucky number.
'Quattor' + '-dici'. Stress on 'tor': 'kwat-TOR-dee-chee'.
From Latin 'quindecim'. Stress on the first syllable: 'KWEEN-dee-chee'.
'Se' (from sei) + '-dici', stress on the first syllable. The last of the 'unit + dici' numbers.
From 17 the order flips: 'dici' (ten) + 'sette'. Note the double 'ss' and double 'tt'. Seventeen is Italy's unlucky number.
'Dici' + 'otto'. Eighteen is the age of majority: 'i diciotto anni' / 'il diciottesimo' is the big birthday party.
'Dici' + 'nove' with a doubled 'nn' in between. Stress on 'no': 'dee-chan-NO-veh'.
Latin 'viginti'. The tens drop their final vowel before 'uno' and 'otto': ventuno, ventotto. Other tens: trenta, quaranta, cinquanta, sessanta, settanta, ottanta, novanta.
Latin 'centum'. Invariable in the plural: duecento, trecento, novecento. 'Per cento' = per cent; English 'cent' and 'century' share the root.
Latin 'mille'. Its plural is irregular: 'duemila', 'diecimila'. 'Grazie mille' = thanks a thousand.
Ordinals agree like adjectives: primo/prima/primi/prime. Then secondo, terzo, quarto, quinto, sesto, settimo, ottavo, nono, decimo; from 11 on add '-esimo': undicesimo.
Latin 'medius'. 'Mezzo chilo' (half a kilo), 'mezz'ora' (half an hour), 'mezzogiorno' (noon, literally mid-day). Agrees: 'mezza'. English borrowed 'mezzo-soprano'.
Latin 'familia'. The 'gli' is one soft sound like 'lli' in 'million'. Feminine; plural 'le famiglie'.
Latin 'mater'; English 'maternal'. In speech 'mamma' is far more common than 'madre'.
Latin 'pater'; English 'paternal'. The informal word is 'papà' or, in Tuscany, 'babbo'.
The everyday word for mother, used by adults too. 'Mamma mia!' is a real exclamation of surprise or dismay.
The accent matters: 'papà' is dad, 'papa' without accent is the Pope.
Latin 'filius'. 'I figli' means children of any sex (sons and daughters), while 'i bambini' means young children in general.
A diminutive of Latin 'frater'; English 'fraternal'. Plural 'i fratelli' can mean 'brothers' or 'siblings'.
A diminutive of Latin 'soror'; English 'sorority'. Plural 'le sorelle'.
'I nonni' = grandparents. Affectionate forms 'nonnino', 'nonnina' are common.
Masculine nouns beginning with 'z' take the article 'lo' (plural 'gli zii'). From Late Latin 'thius', from Greek 'theîos'.
From Latin 'consobrinus', the same source as English 'cousin' via French. Unlike English, the form shows the sex: cugino / cugina.
Latin 'maritus'; English 'marital'. 'Mio marito' – possessives with singular family members take no article.
From Latin 'mulier' (woman). Irregular plural 'le mogli'. 'Mia moglie', no article.
Plural of 'genitore', from Latin 'genitor' (one who begets). Not 'parenti', which means relatives – a classic false friend.
'Bimbo' is a casual variant; English 'bimbo' is this word, borrowed in the early 1900s. Plural 'i bambini' covers mixed groups.
Covers teenagers and young adults; 'il mio ragazzo' = my boyfriend. 'Ragazzi!' is how you address a group, like 'guys'. Note the double 'zz'.
Latin 'homo'. Irregular plural 'gli uomini'. 'Uomo' also means human being: 'i diritti dell'uomo' (human rights).
From Latin 'domina' (mistress of the house); related to 'madonna' (my lady) and 'prima donna', both borrowed by English.
From Late Latin 'companio' (cum + panis, one who shares bread), the source of English 'companion'. 'Il mio compagno' = my partner; 'compagno di classe' = classmate.
One word for grandson, granddaughter, nephew and niece; only the article shows the sex: 'il nipote' / 'la nipote'. English 'nephew' comes from the same Latin 'nepos'.
Before a name the final 'e' drops: 'il signor Rossi', 'la signora Bianchi'. 'Signorina' (Miss) is now used mostly for girls. From Latin 'senior'.
Grammatically singular: 'la gente è gentile' (people are kind). A frequent mistake is to use a plural verb as in English.
Always feminine, even for a man: 'Marco è una persona simpatica'. Plural 'le persone' is the countable word for people.
From 'fidanza' (trust, pledge). Officially 'engaged', but many Italians use it for any serious partner, engaged or not.
Reflexive; 'sposare qualcuno' = to marry someone. From Latin 'sponsare' (to betroth); English 'spouse'. Past participle 'sposato'.
Latin 'panis'. Family of words: 'panino' (roll, sandwich), 'panetteria' (bakery), 'panettone' (the Christmas cake, 'big bread').
Latin 'aqua'; the 'cq' spelling marks a long 'k'. Feminine ('l'' before a vowel). In a restaurant: 'naturale' (still) or 'frizzante' (sparkling).
Latin 'vinum'. 'Vino rosso', 'vino bianco', 'vino della casa' (house wine). 'Vigna' is the vineyard.
Masculine, though it ends in '-e'. Order 'un latte' in Italy and you get a glass of milk: the coffee drink is 'caffellatte' or 'caffè latte'.
From Latin 'formaticum', 'made in a mould' (forma), the same source as French 'fromage'. Older word 'cacio' survives in 'cacio e pepe'.
Latin 'caro, carnis'; English 'carnivore'. 'Carnevale' was traditionally explained as 'carne levare', putting meat away before Lent.
Latin 'piscis'. 'Sc' before 'e' or 'i' sounds like 'sh': 'PEH-sheh'. Plural 'i pesci'; the zodiac sign is 'Pesci'.
A collective singular: 'mangio molta frutta'. 'Il frutto' is one single fruit, or a result ('il frutto del lavoro').
Derived from 'verde' (green). Usually singular as a collective, like 'frutta'; 'le verdure' is also fine for specific vegetables.
Masculine in the singular ('l'uovo', 'un uovo'), feminine in the plural: 'le uova'. A famous irregular. Latin 'ovum'.
From Greek 'oryza' via Latin. 'Riso' also means laughter (from 'ridere'). 'Risotto' is literally 'big rice dish'.
Literally 'dough, paste' (Late Latin 'pasta'). It also means a pastry: 'le paste' at a bar are little cakes. 'Pasta' as a dish is singular.
Latin 'oleum', from 'oliva'. Masculine: 'l'olio d'oliva', 'l'olio extravergine'.
Latin 'sal'. 'Salario' (salary) goes back to Latin 'salarium', linked by the Romans themselves to salt.
Takes 'lo' because it starts with 'z'. From Arabic 'sukkar' via Sicily; 'cch' is a long hard 'k': 'TSOOK-keh-ro'.
Named for the yellow varieties first grown in 16th-century Italy. Plural 'i pomodori'.
From Latin 'melum/malum'. 'Melanzana' (aubergine) is a separate word but was folk-etymologised as 'mela insana', unhealthy apple.
Latin 'pullus' (young animal), the root of English 'poultry' via French. 'Pollo arrosto' = roast chicken.
Borrowed from German 'Bier'; the double 'rr' is rolled long. 'Una birra alla spina' = a draught beer.
From Latin 'collatio' (bringing together). 'Fare colazione' = to have breakfast; typically a cappuccino and a 'cornetto' standing at the bar.
Latin 'prandium'. Traditionally the main meal, eaten around one o'clock. Verb: 'pranzare'.
Latin 'cena'. Verb 'cenare'. Leonardo's Last Supper is 'L'Ultima Cena'. Dinner in Italy is usually after 8 pm.
Shares its source with French 'manger', Latin 'manducare' (to chew). Regular -are verb; the 'i' is dropped before 'i': 'mangi', 'mangiamo'. Past participle 'mangiato'.
Contracted from Latin 'bibere'; the old stem 'bev-' reappears in the present and in the irregular past participle 'bevuto'.
From 'cucina', which means both kitchen and cuisine (Latin 'coquina'). 'Cuocere' is the more technical 'to cook (food through heat)'.
'Un caffè' in Italy is a small espresso, usually drunk standing at the bar. Final accented 'è'; invariable plural 'i caffè'. From Turkish 'kahve', Arabic 'qahwa'.
Named after the brown habit of the Capuchin friars, who took their name from the 'cappuccio' (hood). Italians drink it in the morning, rarely after a meal.
Borrowed from English, but an Italian 'bar' is a daytime café serving coffee, pastries and sandwiches as well as drinks. Invariable: 'i bar'.
From 'ristorare' (to restore, refresh), like French 'restaurant'. Plural 'i ristoranti'.
A simpler, often family-run place with home-style regional cooking; an 'osteria' is similar. The word is used in English for the same thing.
Borrowed from French; written 'menù' or 'menu', invariable in the plural. 'Menù fisso' = set menu, 'il menù del giorno' = today's menu.
Also 'count' and 'bank account'. From Latin 'computus'. 'Il conto, per favore' is the standard way to ask for the bill.
From 'camera' (room), originally a chamber servant. Beware the false friend: 'camera' means room; a photo camera is 'macchina fotografica'.
'Tavolo' is the piece of furniture; 'tavola' is the table laid for a meal: 'A tavola!' (dinner's ready!). 'Un tavolo per due' = a table for two.

example.target: Un tavolo per due, per favore.

note: Plural 'le pizze'. The classic Margherita is Neapolitan; a 'pizzeria' is the place that makes it. Italians order one pizza each, never slices to share.
Past participle of 'gelare' (to freeze). Sold in a 'gelateria', by 'cono' (cone) or 'coppetta' (cup); flavours are 'gusti'.
'Anti-' here is Latin 'ante' (before) + 'pasto' (meal). It has nothing to do with being against pasta.
Short for 'primo piatto': pasta, risotto or soup. An Italian menu runs antipasto, primo, secondo with contorno, dolce.
Short for 'secondo piatto', the meat or fish course. Side dishes ('contorni') are ordered separately.
'Dolce' is the adjective 'sweet' (Latin 'dulcis'), as in 'la dolce vita'. Plural 'i dolci'.
A fixed per-person charge for bread and the table, shown on the bill. It is legal and normal in Italy, not a tip.
Tipping is modest in Italy: rounding up or leaving a few euros is enough, since 'coperto' or 'servizio' are often already charged.
From Latin 'aperire' (to open), as it opens the appetite. An evening ritual: a spritz or a glass of wine with snacks. 'Apericena' is one big enough to replace dinner.
Diminutive of 'pane'. In Italian the plural is 'panini', which English has adopted as a singular.
'Un bicchiere di vino' = a glass of wine. The material glass is 'vetro'. Pronounced 'beek-KYEH-reh'.
From Late Latin 'butticula', the same source as English 'bottle'. 'Una bottiglia d'acqua'.
Also means 'to tidy up' and 'to command'. 'Posso ordinare?' = Can I order? Past participle 'ordinato'.
'Pre-' + 'notare'. 'Ho prenotato un tavolo per le otto' is the sentence to learn. Noun: 'la prenotazione'.
From Latin 'pacare' (to appease, settle). An 'h' keeps the 'g' hard in 'paghi', 'paghiamo'. 'Pagare alla cassa' = pay at the till; 'offro io' = it's on me.
Said to everyone at the table before eating, even by the waiter. Reply 'grazie, altrettanto' (thanks, likewise).
From Latin 'viaticum' (provisions for the road) via Provençal, the same source as English 'voyage'. 'Buon viaggio!' = have a good trip.
From Latin 'vacare' (to be free, empty); English 'vacancy', 'vacation'. Usually plural: 'andare in vacanza', 'le vacanze estive' (summer holidays).

example.en: Where are you going on holiday?

note: Masculine; 'all'aeroporto' = at/to the airport. Note 'aero-' with 'e', not 'air-'.
From a Germanic word for army shelter, cognate with English 'harbour' and French 'auberge'. 'Hotel' is also used, often for bigger places. Plural 'gli alberghi'.
A false friend: 'camera' means room (Latin 'camera', vault), as in 'camera singola / matrimoniale'. A photo camera is 'la macchina fotografica'.

example.en: Do you have a room free?

note: 'Fare la valigia' = to pack. Plural 'le valigie' (or 'valige'); 'bagaglio' is luggage in general.

literal: pass-port (permission to pass through a port)
note: Same build as English 'passport'. 'Carta d'identità' is the ID card Italians use within the EU.
Diminutive of 'carta' (paper, chart). 'Mappa' is also common; 'piantina' is a town plan. 'Carta' alone can also mean a playing card or paper.
Latin 'dextra'. 'Gira a destra' = turn right; 'la destra' is also the political right.
Latin 'sinistra'. English 'sinister' comes from the same word, through the old belief that the left side was unlucky.
The phrase everyone giving directions uses: 'Vai sempre dritto'. 'Dritto' (also 'diritto') comes from Latin 'directus'.
'Vicino a' = near (to). Also a noun, 'il vicino / la vicina' = neighbour. From Latin 'vicinus' (of the village).
'Lontano da' = far from. From Latin 'longe'. 'Da lontano' = from afar.
From Latin '(via) strata', paved road, the same source as English 'street'. 'Via' is the usual word in addresses: 'Via Roma 5'.
From 'uscire' (to go out). 'Uscita di sicurezza' = emergency exit; it is also the motorway exit.
From 'entrare'. On doors you will also see 'ingresso'; 'ingresso libero' = free admission.
'Girare a destra' = turn right. Also 'to shoot (a film)' and 'to wander around': 'girare per la città'. Past participle 'girato'.
From 'viaggio'. Regular -are verb; the stem 'viaggi-' loses nothing before 'i': 'viaggi', 'viaggiamo'. Past participle 'viaggiato'.
Regular -ire verb. Takes 'essere' in the past: 'sono partito/a'. 'Partire per Roma' = to leave for Rome.
From Latin 'ad ripam', 'to the shore', like English 'arrive'. Takes 'essere': 'siamo arrivati'. 'Arrivo!' = coming!
Plural 'le spiagge'. 'Andare in spiaggia' = go to the beach; a 'stabilimento balneare' is a beach club with sunbeds.
Latin 'clavis'; Latin 'cl-' became Italian 'chi-' (also 'chiaro', 'chiesa'). English 'clef' and 'clavicle' share the root. Feminine; plural 'le chiavi'.
Nouns in '-ista' have one form for both sexes; the article shows the gender. Plurals differ: 'i turisti', 'le turiste'.
'Dove' + 'è' elides to 'dov'è'. The most useful question on the road: 'Dov'è la stazione?', 'Dov'è il bagno?'

example.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

note: Reflexive of 'perdere' (to lose). Past participle 'perso' (also 'perduto'): 'Mi sono perso' / 'persa'.
Borrowed from French 'train'. 'Regionale' trains are slow and cheap; 'Frecciarossa' and 'Italo' are high-speed. 'In treno' = by train.

example.en: I'm taking the eight o'clock train.

note: Masculine and invariable: 'gli autobus'. A long-distance coach is a 'pullman', from the American Pullman company.
Literally 'machine', but the everyday word for car; 'automobile' and 'auto' are more formal. 'cch' is a long 'k'. 'In macchina' = by car.
Shortened to 'bici' in speech. 'Andare in bicicletta' = to cycle. Built from 'bi-' + Greek 'kyklos' (wheel) + diminutive.
Latin 'statio'. 'Stazione' alone means railway station; 'stazione di servizio' is a service station, 'stazione dei pullman' the coach station.
From 'fermare' (to stop). 'Fermata dell'autobus'. 'La prossima fermata' = the next stop; the 'fermata a richiesta' stops only on request.
From French 'billet'. Remember to validate it: 'convalidare' or 'timbrare il biglietto' in the yellow or green machine, or risk a fine.

example.target: Un biglietto per Firenze, per favore.

note: From Latin 'binarius' (in twos), for the two rails. Platforms are announced by track: 'Il treno parte dal binario 4'.
Shortened to 'la metro' (feminine). Rome, Milan, Naples, Turin, Genoa, Brescia and Catania have one.
Invariable; also spelled 'tassì'. In Italy taxis are taken from a rank or called, and rarely hailed in the street.
Masculine, short for 'aeroplano'. 'In aereo' = by plane. Note the spelling 'ae-', not 'ai-'.
From 'volare' (to fly), the verb of the famous 1958 song 'Volare'. 'Al volo' = on the fly, quickly.
Latin 'navis'; English 'navy', 'navigate', 'nave' (of a church, shaped like a ship). Plural 'le navi'.
Related to Latin 'traicere' (to carry across), also behind English 'trajectory'. Ferries link the mainland with Sicily, Sardinia and the islands.
Feminine and invariable ('le moto'), short for 'motocicletta'. 'Andare in moto' = ride a motorbike.
From Latin 'patens' (open), as in 'letters patent'. A false friend: a patent for an invention is 'un brevetto'.
'Fare benzina' = to fill up; diesel is 'gasolio' or 'diesel'; the attendant is the 'benzinaio'. 'Benzina verde' = unleaded.
From 'parcheggiare' (to park). 'Divieto di sosta' = no parking; blue lines are paid spaces, white ones free.
Feminine. Italian motorways charge a toll ('pedaggio'); the A1 Milan–Naples is the 'Autostrada del Sole'. Italy opened the world's first motorway in 1924.
Also 'to guide, to lead'; 'la guida' is both a guidebook and driving ('scuola guida' = driving school). Past participle 'guidato'.
'Prendere il treno', 'prendere un caffè'. Irregular past participle 'preso'. Latin 'prehendere'; English 'apprehend', 'prison' share the root.

en: to get on, to go up
note: 'Salire sul treno' = get on the train. Irregular in 'salgo' and 'salgono'. Latin 'salire' meant 'to jump'. Past participle 'salito'.

en: to get off, to go down
note: 'Scendere dal treno' = get off the train. Irregular past participle 'sceso'. 'Sc' before 'e' = 'sh': 'SHEN-deh-reh'.

example.en: I'm getting off at the next stop.

note: The vehicle of Italian teenagers. 'Scooter' is also used; the Vespa, launched in 1946, means 'wasp'.
'In ritardo' = late (for something): 'Il treno è in ritardo di dieci minuti'. Latin 'retardare'; English 'retard', 'tardy'.
Latin 'hora'. 'Che ora è?' = what time is it? Also the adverb 'now' ('ora vado'). Plural 'le ore'.
From Latin 'diurnum' (daily); English 'journal' and 'journey' (originally a day's travel) share the root. 'Giornata' = the day as a span.
From 'sette' (Latin 'septimana', 'of seven'). Weekend is 'il fine settimana' (masculine) or simply 'il weekend'.
Latin 'mensis'. Plural 'i mesi'; 'al mese' = per month. 'Mensile' = monthly.
Latin 'annus'. Say the double 'nn' clearly: 'ano' with one 'n' means anus. 'Ho trent'anni' = I'm thirty (age uses 'avere').
From Latin 'hodie' (this day). 'Oggi pomeriggio' = this afternoon. 'Al giorno d'oggi' = nowadays.
From Latin 'de mane', 'in the morning'. 'Dopodomani' = the day after tomorrow; 'a domani' = see you tomorrow.
Latin 'heri'. 'Ieri sera' = last night; 'l'altro ieri' = the day before yesterday.
Interchangeable with 'ora'. 'Adesso' is slightly more colloquial. 'Proprio adesso' = right now.
Latin 'lunae dies', like English 'Monday'. Days are not capitalised and end in accented '-dì' (day). 'Il lunedì' = on Mondays.
Latin 'Martis dies' (French 'mardi'). The Latin planet names survive in Italian days where English has Norse gods.
Latin 'Mercurii dies'. Stress on the final 'dì', as in all days except sabato and domenica.
Latin 'Iovis dies'. English 'Thursday' swapped Jupiter for the Germanic thunder god Thor.
Latin 'Veneris dies'. 'Venerdì sera' = Friday night.
From Hebrew 'shabbat' via Latin 'sabbatum', like 'Sabbath'. No accent: stress on the first syllable, 'SA-ba-to'.
Latin 'dies dominica'. Stress on the second syllable: 'do-MEH-ni-ca'. Days of the week are all masculine except 'la domenica'.
From Janus, the two-faced god of doorways. Months are not capitalised: gennaio, febbraio, marzo, aprile, maggio, giugno, luglio, agosto, settembre, ottobre, novembre, dicembre.
Named after the emperor Augustus. 'Ferragosto' (15 August, from Latin 'feriae Augusti') is the holiday when much of Italy shuts down.
'Di mattina' / 'la mattina' = in the morning; 'il mattino' also exists. 'Stamattina' = this morning.
'Stasera' = this evening (from 'questa sera'); 'ieri sera' = last night. 'Buona serata' wishes a good evening ahead.
From Latin 'post meridiem', the same words as English 'p.m.'. 'Nel pomeriggio' = in the afternoon.
Answer with 'Sono le tre' (it's three), but singular for one o'clock and noon: 'È l'una', 'È mezzogiorno'. 'Che ora è?' is equally common.

example.target: Che ore sono? – Sono le due e mezza.
example.en: What time is it? – It's half past two.

note: No preposition: 'aspetto il treno' (I'm waiting for the train). The reflexive 'aspettarsi' means 'to expect'. Latin 'exspectare'. Past participle 'aspettato'.
From Latin 'minutus' (small). 'Un minuto!' = just a minute. Also the adjective 'tiny'.
'È tardi' = it's late; 'più tardi' = later; 'a più tardi' = see you later. For being late for something say 'in ritardo'. Latin 'tarde'.
Masculine, unlike French 'couleur'. Latin 'color'. 'Di che colore è?' = what colour is it? Plural 'i colori'.
Latin 'russus'. Double 'ss'. 'Vino rosso', 'Croce Rossa' (Red Cross). Agrees: rosso/rossa/rossi/rosse.
Invariable: 'una macchina blu', 'occhi blu'. From French 'bleu', of Germanic origin. For lighter blues Italians say 'azzurro'.
Latin 'viridis'. One form for masculine and feminine, plural 'verdi' (hence the composer Verdi). 'Verdura' = vegetables.
'Un giallo' also means a detective novel, after the yellow covers of Mondadori's crime series launched in 1929.
Of Germanic origin, like French 'blanc' and English 'blank'. Plurals take an 'h' to keep the hard 'k': bianchi, bianche. 'In bianco' = plain (of food).
Latin 'niger'. 'Nero' is also the noun 'black'. Agrees: nero/nera/neri/nere.
Of Germanic origin, like French 'gris'. Plural 'grigi' (one 'i'), feminine plural 'grigie' or 'grige'.
Originally the noun 'marrone', a large chestnut. Traditionally invariable, but 'marroni' in the plural is now usual. For hair and eyes say 'castano'.
From 'arancia' (the fruit), which came from Arabic 'nāranj' via Persian; English 'orange' has the same source. Plural 'arancioni'.
Invariable, because it is really the noun 'rosa' (rose): 'scarpe rosa'. A 'romanzo rosa' is a romance novel.
Invariable, from the flower 'viola' (violet). Also the string instrument. 'Vestiti viola'.
From Persian 'lāzhward' (lapis lazuli) via Arabic, the same source as English 'azure'. 'Gli Azzurri' are Italy's national sports teams, who play in blue.
Latin 'clarus' ('cl' became 'chi'). 'Verde chiaro' = light green; 'È chiaro?' = is that clear? English borrowed 'chiaroscuro' from Italian painting.
From Latin 'obscurus'. 'Blu scuro' = dark blue; 'al buio' is 'in the dark' (noun 'buio').
Latin 'forma'. 'Essere in forma' = to be fit; 'formaggio' (cheese) was literally 'something shaped in a mould'.
Latin 'circulus'. 'C' before 'e' = 'ch': 'CHER-kyo'. A club or group is 'circolo', a different word from the same root.
From 'quattro'. Also the adjective 'square': 'metro quadrato'. The town square is 'la piazza', not 'quadrato'.
'Tri-' + 'angolo' (angle, corner). 'Angolo' also means corner: 'all'angolo' = on the corner.
Latin 'linea'. Also a bus or phone line ('è caduta la linea' = the line dropped) and one's figure ('mantenere la linea').
Latin 'rotundus', from 'rota' (wheel); English 'rotund', 'rotunda'. 'Tavolo rotondo' = round table.
Latin 'punctum'. 'Punto e basta' = full stop, end of story. 'A che punto sei?' = how far have you got?
Latin 'stella'. 'Stellato' = starry; a chef with 'tre stelle Michelin'. 'Stellina' is a term of endearment.
'Retto' (right, straight) + 'angolo'. 'Angolo retto' = right angle.
Latin 'crux'. 'C' before 'e' = 'ch': 'KRO-cheh'. 'Croce Rossa' = Red Cross; 'a croce' = cross-shaped.
Latin 'corpus'; English 'corpse', 'corporal', 'corporation'. 'Corpo' also means a corps.
From Latin 'testa' (pot, shell), Roman slang for head, like 'noggin'. The older 'capo' (Latin 'caput') now means boss or chief.
Latin 'oculus'. 'cch' is a long 'k': 'OK-kyo'. Plural 'gli occhi'; glasses are 'gli occhiali'. 'Occhio!' = watch out!
Latin 'nasus'. 'Avere naso' = to have a good nose, flair. Plural 'i nasi'.
Latin 'bucca' (cheek), which replaced 'os'. 'In bocca al lupo' = good luck; 'acqua in bocca!' = keep it secret.
Latin 'auricula'. Two plurals exist: 'gli orecchi' and 'le orecchie'. 'Orecchiette' pasta are 'little ears'.
Feminine despite the '-o', because Latin 'manus' was feminine; plural 'le mani'. 'Dare una mano' = to lend a hand.
Masculine singular, but the pair is feminine 'le braccia' (Latin neuter plural). 'I bracci' is used for arms of a chair or a river.
From Late Latin 'gamba' (hoof), also behind French 'jambe'. 'In gamba' = capable, on the ball: 'una persona in gamba'.
Latin 'pes, pedis'; English 'pedal', 'pedestrian'. 'A piedi' = on foot. Plural 'i piedi'.
'Mal di pancia' = stomach ache. 'Pancetta' (bacon) is literally 'little belly'. The anatomical stomach is 'lo stomaco'.
Latin 'dens'; English 'dentist'. Pasta 'al dente' is cooked 'to the tooth', still firm. Plural 'i denti'.
Plural; 'un capello' is a single hair. Do not double the 'p': 'cappello' is a hat. Body hair is 'peli'.
'Sch' = 'sk': 'SKYEH-na'. 'Mal di schiena' = backache. Of Germanic origin, related to English 'shin'.
Latin 'cor'; English 'cordial', 'courage'. 'Di cuore' = heartily; 'ti ringrazio di cuore'. Pronounced 'KWO-reh'.
Any university graduate may be addressed as 'dottore'/'dottoressa'; a physician is also 'il medico'. Before a name: 'il dottor Rossi'.
Latin 'hospitale', the same root as 'hotel', 'hostel' and 'hospitality'. Masculine. A&E is 'il pronto soccorso'.
Stress on the 'i': 'far-ma-CHEE-a'. Marked by a green cross; the 'farmacia di turno' is the one open out of hours.
'Prendere una medicina' = to take a medicine. Also the field of study; 'medicinale' is the formal word for a drug.
'Mal di' + body part is the pattern: 'mal di gola' (sore throat), 'mal di pancia', 'mal di schiena'. 'Ho mal di testa' = I have a headache.
Latin 'febris'; English 'febrile'. Double 'bb'. 'Avere la febbre' = to have a temperature.
From 'male' (badly, ill). Also a noun, 'il malato' = the patient. 'Ammalarsi' = to fall ill.

example.en: I've been ill for three days.

note: Latin 'salus'. 'Salute!' is both 'cheers!' and 'bless you!' after a sneeze. Related to 'salve' and 'salvo' (safe).
Latin 'dormire'; English 'dormitory', 'dormant'. Regular -ire verb. Past participle 'dormito'.
From 'freddo' (cold) via 'raffreddare' (to cool). 'Avere il raffreddore' = to have a cold; 'avere freddo' = to feel cold.
Latin 'casa' (hut) replaced 'domus'. 'A casa' = at home / home, with no article: 'vado a casa'. Also 'company' in brand names ('Casa Barilla').
Means both the room and the cuisine: 'la cucina italiana'. From Latin 'coquina'; 'cucinare' is the verb.
'Camera' alone already means (bed)room in hotels; 'da' marks purpose, as in 'occhiali da sole', 'costume da bagno'.
Latin 'balneum'. 'Fare il bagno' = to have a bath or to go for a swim. 'Dov'è il bagno?' is the polite way to ask for the toilet.
From 'soggiornare' (to stay). The same word is the 'permesso di soggiorno', the residence permit. 'Salotto' is the cosier word for a sitting room.
Latin 'porta' (gate). 'Portone' is the big street door of a building; 'portiere' is the doorman and the goalkeeper.
Latin 'fenestra', the word behind English 'defenestrate'. 'Finestrino' is a car or train window.
Latin 'lectus'. Identical to 'letto', past participle of 'leggere' (read). 'Andare a letto' = go to bed; 'camera da letto' = bedroom.
From Latin 'sedes' (seat); 'sedersi' = to sit down. 'Sedia a rotelle' = wheelchair.
From Turkish 'divan', originally a council chamber with low couches; English 'divan' is the same word. 'Divano letto' = sofa bed.
From Greek 'lampas' via Latin. A light bulb is 'la lampadina', the diminutive.
From Latin 'frigus' (cold) + '-fero' (bearing). Nearly always shortened to 'il frigo' in speech.
'Fare la doccia' = to take a shower. Originally a water pipe; English 'douche' came from it through French. Plural 'le docce'.
Of Germanic origin, like French 'jardin' and English 'garden'. 'Giardino pubblico' = park; a vegetable garden is 'l'orto'.
'Piano terra' = ground floor, 'primo piano' = first floor above it. Also 'flat', 'plan', and 'softly' in music: English 'piano' is short for 'pianoforte' (soft-loud).

example.en: I live on the third floor.

note: Masculine, from 'ascendere' (to go up). 'Prendere l'ascensore' = take the lift.
Usually 'la tivù' or 'la TV' in speech; the set itself is 'il televisore'. 'Guardare la televisione'.
Latin 'furnus'; English 'furnace'. 'Al forno' = baked ('pasta al forno'); 'forno a microonde' = microwave; the bakery is 'il forno' or 'il fornaio'.
Both the plate and the dish served on it ('primo piatto'). Also the adjective 'flat'. 'Lavare i piatti' = do the dishes.
From 'stare' (to stay). English 'stanza' in poetry is this word, a 'stopping place'. 'Camera' is specifically a bedroom.
From Latin 'armarium', a cupboard for tools or arms. 'Armadietto' = locker, cabinet. Masculine; plural 'gli armadi'.
Latin 'speculum'. Takes 'lo' because it begins with 's' + consonant. 'Specchiarsi' = to look at oneself in the mirror.
'Abito a Roma' = I live in Rome; 'vivere' is to live in the broad sense. Latin 'habitare'. 'Abito' is also the noun 'suit, dress'. Past participle 'abitato'.
An '-isc-' verb: the infix appears in all persons except 'noi' and 'voi'. 'Pulito' = clean (adjective). Related to Latin 'polire' (to polish).
Masculine. English 'apartment' came through French from Italian 'appartamento', 'a separated-off part'. 'Monolocale' = studio flat.
Plural of 'vestito'. Also 'i vestiti' = outfits; 'abbigliamento' is clothing as a category or shop section.
A woman's dress or a man's suit; context decides. From 'vestire' (Latin 'vestis', garment). 'Vestito da sera' = evening dress.
From Late Latin 'camisia', the source of 'chemise' and 'camisole'. Plural 'le camicie'. A blouse is 'camicetta'.
Diminutive of 'maglia' (knitwear, jersey). 'Maglia' is also a sports shirt: the 'maglia rosa' is worn by the Giro d'Italia leader.
Named after Pantalone, the Venetian commedia dell'arte character who wore them; English 'pants' and 'pantaloons' come from the same name.
From Late Latin 'gunna', also the origin of English 'gown'. 'Minigonna' = miniskirt.
From French 'jaque'. Plural 'le giacche' (with 'h'). 'Giacca a vento' = windbreaker.
From 'cappa' (cape, cloak). Double 'pp' and double 'tt'. 'Giubbotto' is a short padded jacket.
Singular 'la scarpa'. 'Scarpe da ginnastica' = trainers. Shoe size is 'il numero', not 'la taglia'.
Double 'pp': 'capello' with one 'p' is a hair. Both go back to Latin 'cappa'. 'Tanto di cappello' = hats off.
Also the stock exchange ('la Borsa', from the Van der Buerse house in Bruges, hence 'bourse') and 'borsa di studio' = scholarship.
'Sci' = 'sh': 'SHAR-pa'. From French 'écharpe'. A light silk or cotton scarf is 'il foulard'.
Singular 'il guanto'. Of Germanic origin, like French 'gant'. 'Calzare come un guanto' = to fit like a glove.
Diminutive of 'calza' (stocking). On the night before Epiphany the Befana fills children's 'calze' with sweets or coal.
Latin 'cinctura'. 'Cintura di sicurezza' = seatbelt; 'cintura nera' = black belt.
Usually just 'il costume'. 'Costume' also means custom and fancy-dress costume.
Plural, from 'occhio' (eye). 'Occhiali da sole' = sunglasses, 'occhiali da vista' = prescription glasses.
From 'tagliare' (to cut). 'Che taglia porti?' = what size are you? For shoes use 'numero'.
'Maglia' + the augmentative '-one'. Italian suffixes grade clothes: maglietta (small), maglia, maglione (big).
From Greek 'hōrológion' (hour-teller) via Latin. Masculine. 'Orologio da polso' = wristwatch; plural 'gli orologi'.
Reflexive of 'vestire'. 'Vestirsi bene' = to dress well. Past participle 'vestito', which doubles as the noun 'dress'.
From 'in dosso' (on the back, Latin 'dorsum'). 'Portare' is used just as often for wearing: 'porta gli occhiali'. Past participle 'indossato'.
From 'Croato' (Croat): 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in France wore knotted neckcloths. English 'cravat' is the same word.
Latin 'modus' (manner). 'Alla moda' / 'di moda' = fashionable; 'fuori moda' = out of fashion. Milan is Italy's fashion capital.
One form for both genders; plural 'eleganti'. Dressing well is part of 'fare bella figura', making a good impression.
Latin 'labor'. 'Al lavoro' = at work. 'Buon lavoro!' is a common wish when someone starts their working day.
Regular -are verb. 'Lavorare sodo' = to work hard; 'lavorare da casa' = to work from home. Past participle 'lavorato'.
Latin 'officium' (duty). Masculine; plural 'gli uffici'. 'Ufficio postale' = post office; 'in ufficio' = at the office.
Latin 'schola', from Greek 'scholē' (leisure). 'A scuola' = at school. Stages: elementare, media, superiore.
Feminine and invariable, like all nouns ending in an accented vowel: 'le università'. 'All'università' = at university.
'Lo' before 's' + consonant; plural 'gli studenti'. The feminine adds '-essa', as in 'dottoressa', 'professoressa'.
From 'insegnare'. One form for both sexes; the article shows the gender: 'un insegnante' / 'un'insegnante'. 'Maestro/a' is a primary teacher.
Used for secondary-school teachers as well as academics; pupils just say 'prof'. Before a name the 'e' drops: 'il professor Bianchi'.
The 'i' of the stem merges before 'i': 'studi', 'studiamo'. 'Studio' is also a noun: study, office, studio. Past participle 'studiato'.

example.en: I've been studying Italian for a year.

note: From Latin 'in' + 'parare' (to procure). 'Imparare a memoria' = to learn by heart. Past participle 'imparato'.
From Latin 'insignare' (to mark). 'Gn' is the 'ny' sound. Past participle 'insegnato'.
'Gg' is hard in 'leggo', 'leggono' and soft ('j') in 'leggi', 'legge'. Irregular past participle 'letto', identical to the word for bed. Latin 'legere'.
Latin 'scribere'. Irregular past participle 'scritto' (the 'pt' of 'scriptum' became 'tt'). 'Scrittore' = writer.
Latin 'liber', originally the inner bark of a tree used for writing. Plural 'i libri'. 'Libretto' (little book) is the text of an opera.
Latin 'penna' (feather), since pens were quills. 'Penne' pasta are cut like quill tips. Double 'nn'.
Masculine. 'Dare' or 'sostenere un esame' = to sit an exam; 'superare' = to pass. The school-leaving exam is 'la maturità'.
Latin 'lectio' (a reading). 'Avere lezione' = to have class; 'lezione di italiano' = Italian lesson.
Ends in '-a' but is masculine for men; the article shows the sex. Plurals: 'i colleghi', 'le colleghe'.
Latin 'caput' (head). 'Capo' = chief, boss, head of anything; also 'end' ('da capo' in music = from the top). The feminine 'la capa' is colloquial.
From 'riunire' (to gather, reunite). 'Essere in riunione' = to be in a meeting.
Latin 'stipendium', a soldier's pay; English 'stipend'. 'Lo' before 'st'. Also 'salario', used mostly for wages.
Borrowed from English and invariable: 'i computer'. Pronounced roughly 'com-PYOO-ter'. A laptop is 'il portatile'.
Latin 'lingua': both the organ and the language, as in old English 'tongue'. 'Madrelingua' = native speaker/language.
From Latin 'parabola' (comparison, speech), the same source as 'parable' and 'parole'. 'Parola d'ordine' = password, watchword.
A false friend: a library is 'la biblioteca'. 'Libreria' is where books are sold, or the shelves at home.
Latin 'tempus'. Means both weather ('che tempo fa?') and time ('non ho tempo'). English borrowed 'tempo' from Italian music.
Latin 'sol'. 'C'è il sole' = it's sunny; 'prendere il sole' = to sunbathe. Masculine.
From Latin 'pluvia'. 'Gg' is soft: 'PYOD-ja'. Plural 'le piogge'.
Latin 'ventus'. 'C'è vento' or 'tira vento' = it's windy. 'Ventilatore' = fan.
Latin 'nix, nivis'. 'Nevada' and 'Sierra Nevada' are Spanish cousins. 'Nevicare' = to snow.
From Latin 'nubila'. 'Nuvoloso' = cloudy. 'Avere la testa fra le nuvole' = to have one's head in the clouds.
Latin 'caelum'. 'C' before 'ie' = 'ch': 'CHEH-lo'. 'Santo cielo!' = good heavens!
Latin 'mare'. Masculine, unlike French 'la mer'. 'Al mare' = at the seaside; 'frutti di mare' = seafood.

example.en: In summer we go to the seaside.

note: 'Gn' = 'ny': 'mon-TA-nya'. 'In montagna' = in the mountains. 'Monte' is used in names: Monte Bianco.
Latin 'flumen'. Latin 'fl-' became Italian 'fi-', also in 'fiore' and 'fiamma'. Plural 'i fiumi'.
Latin 'lacus'. Plural 'i laghi' keeps the hard 'g' with an 'h'. Lago di Como, Lago di Garda.
From Latin 'arbor': the first 'r' turned into 'l'. Masculine; 'albero di Natale' = Christmas tree.
Latin 'flos, florem'; 'fl-' > 'fi-'. Florence's Italian name 'Firenze' shows the same change (Latin 'Florentia'). Plural 'i fiori'.
Masculine; plural 'gli animali'. From Latin 'anima' (breath, soul). 'Animale domestico' = pet.
Latin 'canis'; English 'canine'. Plural 'i cani'. 'Attenti al cane' = beware of the dog.
Late Latin 'cattus'. 'Gattino' = kitten. 'Qui gatta ci cova' = something fishy is going on (literally, a cat is brooding here).
A false friend: 'caldo' is hot, not cold (Latin 'calidus'). 'Fa caldo' = it's hot; 'ho caldo' = I'm hot. Also the noun 'heat'.
Latin 'frigidus'. 'Fa freddo' = it's cold; 'ho freddo' = I'm cold (with 'avere', not 'essere'). 'A freddo' = cold, unprepared.
Impersonal, used in the third person. Latin 'pluere'. 'Piove a dirotto' = it's pouring. Past participle 'piovuto', with 'essere' or 'avere'.

example.en: It's been raining since this morning.

note: Impersonal, from 'neve'. The 'h' keeps the 'c' hard in 'nevicherà'. 'Una nevicata' = a snowfall.
Weather uses 'fare': 'fa bel tempo', 'fa brutto tempo', 'fa caldo', 'fa freddo'. 'C'è' is used for sun, wind and fog: 'c'è il sole'.
From Latin 'primo vere' (at the start of spring, 'ver'). Vivaldi's concerto. 'In primavera' = in spring.
Feminine, from Latin 'aestas'. 'In estate' or 'd'estate' = in summer; 'estivo' = summer (adjective).
Masculine, Latin 'autumnus'. Note the double 'nn'. 'In autunno' = in autumn.
Masculine, from Latin 'hibernum (tempus)', the root of English 'hibernate'. 'D'inverno' = in winter.
Latin 'negotium', literally 'not leisure', i.e. business; English 'negotiate'. Plural 'i negozi'. 'Negozio di scarpe' = shoe shop.
Latin 'mercatus'. Most towns have a weekly street market. 'A buon mercato' = cheap; 'mercato nero' = black market.
'Super' + 'mercato'. Plural 'i supermercati'. 'Fare la spesa' = to do the grocery shopping; 'fare spese' = to go shopping for other things.
Plural. A 'soldo' was a coin, from Latin 'solidus', the root of 'soldier' (one paid in solidi). 'Denaro' is the more formal word.
Latin 'pretium'. 'Zz' = 'ts'. 'A metà prezzo' = half price; 'prezzo fisso' = fixed price.
Mostly third person: 'costa', 'costano'. Takes 'essere' in the past: 'è costato caro' (it cost a lot). Latin 'constare'.
From Latin 'comparare' (to procure). Regular -are verb; past participle 'comprato'. 'Comprare' also 'to bribe'.
Latin 'vendere'. 'Vendesi' on a sign = for sale. Past participle 'venduto'; 'vendita' = sale.
Only for money; time is 'passare'. Irregular past participle 'speso'. 'Spendere una fortuna' = to spend a fortune.
'Pagare con la carta' = pay by card. A debit card and the cash machine are both called 'il bancomat' in everyday speech.
From 'contare' (to count): money counted out. 'In contanti' = in cash. Plural noun.
Also the ordinal 'hundredth'. Prices: 'due euro e cinquanta (centesimi)'. 'Cent' is used too.
Masculine and invariable in Italian: 'dieci euro', never 'euri'. Italy adopted it in 2002; the lira was the previous currency.
Latin 'carus'. Both 'expensive' ('troppo caro') and 'dear' ('cara Anna', 'caro amico'). 'Costare caro' = to cost dearly.
Also 'economic(al)'. Plural 'economici' / 'economiche'. 'A buon mercato' is the alternative; there is no exact word for 'cheap'.
'Lo' before 'sc'. 'Fare uno sconto' = to give a discount; 'Mi fa uno sconto?' = can you give me a discount? Related to English 'discount'.
Plural. Italy's regulated sales run in January and July. Singular 'il saldo' means a balance or final payment.
Latin 'capsa' (box); English 'cash' came from it via French 'caisse'. 'Alla cassa' = at the till; 'cassiere/a' = cashier.
'Lo' before 'sc'. Shops must issue one and customers were once fined for leaving without it. A formal receipt is 'ricevuta'; an invoice 'fattura'.
Plural 'Quanto costano?'. 'Quant'è?' (how much is it?) is the short form used when paying.
'Fare un regalo' = to give a present; the verb is 'regalare'. 'È un regalo' can also mean 'it's a bargain'.
'Un paio di scarpe', but also loosely 'un paio di giorni' = a couple of days. Irregular feminine plural 'le paia'.
Irregular past participle of 'aprire'. Shop signs say APERTO / CHIUSO. 'All'aperto' = outdoors.
Irregular past participle of 'chiudere'. 'Chiuso per ferie' = closed for holidays, a common August sign. 'Chi' = 'k': 'KYOO-zo'.
Marked by a white 'T' sign. Sells not just tobacco but stamps, bus tickets, phone top-ups and lottery tickets; the owner is 'il tabaccaio'.
Latin 'felix'. One form for both genders; plural 'felici'. 'Felice' is a bit stronger than 'contento'; both are everyday.
Latin 'tristis'. One form; plural 'tristi'. 'Tristezza' = sadness.
Latin 'contentus' (satisfied). The usual word for being happy about something: 'sono contento di vederti'.
From 'rabbia' (rage; also rabies, Latin 'rabies'). 'Penne all'arrabbiata' is pasta in an 'angry', hot chilli sauce.
'Stanco morto' = dead tired. Plurals take 'h': 'stanchi', 'stanche'. 'Stancarsi' = to get tired.

example.en: I'm tired, I'm going to bed.

note: From Latin 'pavor'. 'Che paura!' = how scary! 'Fare paura' = to frighten; 'film di paura' = horror film.
Like 'avere fame', 'sete', 'freddo', 'sonno': states are 'had', not 'been'. 'Ho paura di' + noun or infinitive.
Masculine, Latin 'amor'. 'Amore' is also what couples and parents call each other: 'amore mio'. Plural 'gli amori'.
'Ti amo' is reserved for romantic love; to family and friends Italians say 'ti voglio bene'. Regular -are; past participle 'amato'.
'Piacere' works backwards: the thing liked is the subject, the person is an indirect object. Plural things take 'piacciono': 'mi piacciono i gatti'. Past participle 'piaciuto'.
An '-isc-' verb like 'capire' and 'finire'. Past participle 'preferito', which is also the adjective 'favourite'.
Often closer to 'irritable, tense' than to 'anxious': 'oggi sono nervoso' can mean 'I'm on edge today'. 'Ansioso' = anxious.
'Tranquillo!' or 'Stai tranquillo' = relax, don't worry. Double 'll'. Latin 'tranquillus'.

example.en: Don't worry, I'll be right there.

note: A false friend: from 'noia' (boredom), so it means bored, not annoyed. 'Annoyed' is 'seccato' or 'infastidito'. English 'annoy' and 'noia' do share a Latin root.
Irregular past participle of 'sorprendere' (compare 'preso' from 'prendere'). 'Una sorpresa' = a surprise.
From Latin 'gaudia'. 'Che gioia!' = what a joy! Also a term of endearment: 'gioia mia'.
Latin 'ridere'; English 'ridiculous'. Irregular past participle 'riso', the same as the word for rice. 'Ridere di' = to laugh at.
Latin 'plangere' (to beat one's breast); 'pl-' became 'pi-'. Irregular past participle 'pianto'. 'Piangere' has 'gn' only in spelling, not the 'ny' sound.
Built on 'amore': 'innamorato di' = in love with. The verb 'innamorarsi' = to fall in love. Double 'nn'.
From 'preoccupare'. 'Non ti preoccupare' / 'non si preoccupi' = don't worry. Noun 'preoccupazione'.
Latin 'felicitas'. Nouns in '-tà' are feminine and invariable; the accent replaces the Latin '-tate' ending (also 'città', 'università').

en: to miss (be missed by); to be lacking
note: Inverted like 'piacere': 'mi manchi' = I miss you (you are lacking to me); 'mi manca l'Italia' = I miss Italy. The 'h' keeps the 'c' hard.
Said with a shrug and a pout. Extremely common in speech, never in formal writing. 'Mah' is the thoughtful cousin ('well, hmm').
Love for family, friends and partners alike; 'ti amo' is only romantic. Texters shorten it to 'TVB'.
Latin 'zelosus'. 'Gelosia' is also a slatted window blind (you can watch unseen); English borrowed it as 'jalousie'.
For people and places ('conosco Roma'); facts take 'sapere'. 'Sc' before 'e/i' = 'sh', before 'o' = 'sk': 'conosco' vs 'conosci'. Past participle 'conosciuto'.
The 'h' is silent and only distinguishes 'ho/o', 'hai/ai', 'ha/a', 'hanno/anno'. Also used for age and sensations: 'ho vent'anni', 'ho fame'. Past participle 'avuto'.
Latin 'facere'; irregular past participle 'fatto'. An all-purpose verb: 'fare colazione', 'fare la spesa', 'fare una foto', 'fa caldo'.
Mixes two Latin verbs: 'vado, vai, va, vanno' from 'vadere', the rest from 'andare'. Takes 'essere' in the past: 'sono andato'.
Irregular: 'vengo', 'vengono'. Past participle 'venuto', with 'essere'. 'Vengo!' = coming! Latin 'venire'.
'Come stai?' and 'sto bene' use 'stare'. Also forms the progressive: 'sto mangiando'. Past participle 'stato', shared with 'essere'.
'Posso?' = may I? Past participle 'potuto'. Also the noun 'power'; English 'potent'.
'Voglio' is blunt; the conditional 'vorrei' (I'd like) is the polite form for ordering. Past participle 'voluto'. 'Volere bene' = to love.
Also the noun 'duty'. 'Devo' has the variant 'debbo'. Past participle 'dovuto'. 'Dovere' + infinitive: 'devo andare'.
'So nuotare' = I can swim (know how). Facts and skills take 'sapere'; people and places take 'conoscere'. Past participle 'saputo'.
Contracted from Latin 'dicere', so the stem 'dic-' returns in 'dico', 'dici'. Irregular past participle 'detto'. 'Come si dice...?' = how do you say...?
Irregular past participle 'visto' (also 'veduto'). 'Ci vediamo!' = see you! Latin 'videre'; English 'video'.
'Dà' takes an accent to differ from 'da' (from). Past participle 'dato'. 'Dare del tu' = to address someone with 'tu'.
Irregular stem 'esc-' in four forms. Takes 'essere' in the past: 'sono uscito'. 'Uscire con' = to go out with.
From 'parola'. 'Parla inglese?' = do you speak English? 'Parlare di' = to talk about. Past participle 'parlato'.
An '-isc-' verb. 'Non capisco' is a survival phrase; 'Capito?' = got it? Past participle 'capito'. From Latin 'capere' (to grasp).
From Latin 'pensare' (to weigh); English 'pensive'. 'Pensare a' = to think about; 'penso di sì' = I think so.
Reflexive of 'alzare' (to lift). 'Mi alzo alle sette' = I get up at seven. Past participle 'alzato': 'mi sono alzato/a'.
'Mi chiamo Anna' = my name is Anna. 'Come ti chiami?' / 'Come si chiama?' asks the name. Non-reflexive 'chiamare' = to call, phone.
Latin 'aperire'. Regular present, irregular past participle 'aperto'. 'Apre alle nove' = it opens at nine.
Latin 'claudere', the root of 'chiave' (key) and English 'include'. Irregular past participle 'chiuso'.
Irregular past participle 'messo'. 'Mettersi' = to put on (clothes); 'ci mette un'ora' = it takes him an hour. Latin 'mittere' (to send).
No preposition: 'cerco le chiavi'. An 'h' keeps the 'c' hard in 'cerchi', 'cerchiamo'. 'Cercare di' = to try to. English 'search' is a cousin.
'Trovarsi' = to be located, or to feel: 'come ti trovi a Roma?' (how are you finding Rome?). Past participle 'trovato'.
An '-isc-' verb. 'Finire di' + infinitive = to finish doing. Past participle 'finito'; 'è finita' = it's over.
Latin 'qui'. Invariable: 'chi è?', 'chi sono?'. Also 'he who / whoever': 'chi dorme non piglia pesci' (the early bird...).
Short for 'che cosa' (what thing); 'cosa' is also the noun 'thing'. 'Che' alone works too: 'che fai?'.
From Latin 'de ubi'. 'Di dove sei?' = where are you from? Elides before 'è': 'dov'è'.
Latin 'quando'. Also the conjunction 'when': 'quando arrivi, chiamami'. 'Da quando?' = since when?
One word for both 'why' and 'because'. Written with an acute accent (closed 'e'), like 'poiché', 'affinché'.
From Latin 'quomodo'. 'Come?' = pardon?; 'come mai?' = how come?; 'come me' = like me.
Agrees as an adjective: 'quanti anni', 'quante persone'. Invariable as an adverb: 'quanto costa?'.
Plural 'quali'. 'Qual è?' is written without an apostrophe, a point Italians themselves argue about. 'Quale' never elides.
From Latin 'sic' (thus). The accent is compulsory: 'si' without it is the reflexive pronoun. Dante called Italian 'la lingua del sì'.
At the end of a sentence it works as a tag: 'Vieni anche tu, no?' (you're coming too, right?). 'No' alone is a full answer; 'non' negates verbs.
Goes right before the verb: 'non capisco'. Double negatives are correct: 'non ho visto niente' (I didn't see anything).
No accent: 'è' with the accent is 'is'. Often 'ed' before a vowel, especially another 'e': 'ed è'.
From Latin 'magis' (more). 'Ma dai!' = come on!; 'ma va'!' = no way! Also a filler at the start of a sentence.
Goes before the word it refers to: 'anche io' (often 'anch'io') = me too. 'Neanche' = not even, neither.
Invariable as an adverb ('molto bella'), but it agrees as an adjective ('molta gente', 'molti amici'). Opposite: 'poco'.
Latin 'semper'. 'Per sempre' = forever; 'sempre dritto' = straight on; 'come sempre' = as always.
Needs 'non' before the verb: 'non vado mai'. In questions it means 'ever': 'sei mai stato a Roma?'. 'Mai più' = never again.
'Qua' is a looser 'around here'; 'lì' and 'là' mean 'there'. 'Qui vicino' = near here. Latin 'hic' was replaced by 'eccum hic'.
Latin 'cum'. 'Con me', 'con te'. Joins the article in 'col' (con il), now mostly in set phrases.
'Senza zucchero' = without sugar; 'senza dubbio' = no doubt; 'senz'altro' = certainly.
Lowercase, unlike English 'I'. Usually dropped, since the verb ending shows the person; used for emphasis: 'io pago' (I'll pay).
For friends, family, children and peers. 'Dare del tu' = to be on 'tu' terms; it is normal to ask 'possiamo darci del tu?'.
Capitalised in writing to differ from 'lei' (she); the verb is third person singular: 'Lei è inglese?'. Used with strangers, officials and older people.
'Ci' (there) + 'è'; plural 'ci sono'. 'Che c'è?' = what's up?; 'Non c'è' = he's not in; 'c'è il sole' = it's sunny.

example.en: Is there a pharmacy near here?

note: From Latin 'ad illam horam' (at that hour), so also 'at that time'. A universal filler and sentence opener: 'Allora, cosa facciamo?'.
One form for both genders; plural 'grandi'. Often shortened to 'gran' before a noun: 'un gran bel film'. Latin 'grandis'.
'Piccolino' = tiny, cute. 'Da piccolo' = as a child. Plural 'piccoli' / 'piccole'.
Before a noun it changes like the definite article: bel ragazzo, bell'uomo, bello zaino, bei libri, begli occhi, belle case. Latin 'bellus'.
Latin 'brutus'. Also 'bad': 'brutto tempo' (bad weather), 'una brutta figura' (a bad impression). Double 'tt'.
Becomes 'buon' before most masculine nouns: 'buon giorno', 'buon appetito'. Of food it means tasty. People who are good at things are 'bravo'.
From Latin 'captivus' (captive, i.e. of the devil); English 'captive' and 'caitiff'. Of food: 'cattivo' = bad-tasting; 'cattivo odore' = bad smell.
Latin 'novus'. 'Di nuovo' = again. Do not mix up with 'nove' (nine).
'Cch' = long 'k'. For people 'anziano' is more polite. Plural 'vecchi' / 'vecchie'. Latin 'vetulus'.
One form; plural 'giovani'. 'I giovani' = young people. Latin 'iuvenis'; English 'juvenile'.
Plural 'lunghi' keeps the hard 'g'. Also the preposition 'along': 'lungo il fiume'. 'A lungo' = for a long time.
Latin 'curtus'; English 'curt'. For a short person use 'basso'. 'Pantaloni corti' = shorts.
Latin 'altus'; English 'altitude'. 'Alta stagione' = high season; 'ad alta voce' = aloud.
'A bassa voce' = quietly. English 'bass' (the musical range) is the Italian 'basso'.
Latin 'facilis', 'doable' (from 'facere'). One form; plural 'facili'. Stress on the first syllable: 'FA-chi-le'.
Stress on the second syllable: 'dif-FI-chi-le'. One form; plural 'difficili'. Double 'ff'.
Latin 'velox'; English 'velocity'. One form; plural 'veloci'. 'C' before 'e' = 'ch': 'veh-LO-cheh'.
Latin 'lentus'. English uses 'lento' as a musical tempo. 'Lentamente' = slowly.
One form; plural 'forti'. 'Parla più forte' = speak louder. As slang 'forte!' = cool! Latin 'fortis'.
A false friend: not 'sympathetic' (that is 'comprensivo'). The compliment Italians most often pay a person. Plural 'simpatici' / 'simpatiche'.

example.target: I tuoi amici sono molto simpatici.

note: One form; plural 'gentili'. 'Molto gentile' = very kind of you. 'Gentile Signora' opens a formal letter. Latin 'gentilis'.
Plural 'ricchi' / 'ricche' with 'h'. 'Ricco di' = rich in. Of Germanic origin, like English 'rich'.
Position changes meaning: 'un pover'uomo' = a poor (pitiable) man; 'un uomo povero' = a man without money. Latin 'pauper'.
Latin 'plenus'; 'pl-' > 'pi-'. 'Pieno di' = full of; 'fare il pieno' = fill up the tank; 'in pieno centro' = right in the centre.
Also the noun 'il vuoto' (void, empty bottle: 'vuoto a rendere' = returnable). 'A vuoto' = in vain.
'Bravo!' agrees with the person: 'Brava!' to a woman, 'Bravi!' to a group. 'Bravo in matematica' = good at maths.
Latin 'civitas'. Feminine and invariable: 'le città'. 'Cittadino' = citizen; 'in città' = in town.
Both a village and a nation: 'il mio paese' can be either. 'Il Bel Paese' is Italy itself; 'paesaggio' = landscape.

example.en: I come from a small village.

note: 'In centro' = in the town centre; 'centro storico' = the historic centre; 'centro commerciale' = shopping mall.
From Latin 'platea', the same source as 'place' and 'plaza'. The social heart of every Italian town; English borrowed 'piazza'.
Latin 'via' (road). Addresses: 'Via Garibaldi 12'. 'Per via di' = because of; 'via!' = go away!
From Greek 'ekklēsía' via Latin 'ecclesia'; 'chi' = 'k': 'KYEH-za'. 'Andare in chiesa' = go to church.
From Greek 'mouseîon', seat of the Muses. Stress on the 'e': 'mu-ZEH-o'. Plural 'i musei'.
Latin 'pons'. 'Fare il ponte' = to take the day between a holiday and the weekend off, 'bridging' them.
Plural 'i parchi' with 'h'. 'Parco giochi' = playground; 'parco nazionale' = national park.
Latin 'castellum'. 'Castelli in aria' = castles in the air. Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome uses the shortened 'castel'.
From the Germanic word for bench, where moneychangers sat. 'Banca rotta' (broken bench) gave English 'bankrupt'. Plural 'le banche'.
Also simply 'la posta'. Run by Poste Italiane; stamps ('francobolli') are also sold at the tabaccheria.
From the Palatine Hill ('Palatium') in Rome. Any large building, including an ordinary block of flats, not just a palace.
From Latin 'domus (Dei)', house of God: the main church of a city, as in Milan and Florence. Not 'dome' (that is 'cupola'), though English 'dome' came from it.
From Greek 'théatron'. Milan's La Scala is 'il Teatro alla Scala'. 'Fare teatro' = to make a scene.
Masculine and invariable ('i cinema'), short for 'cinematografo'. 'Andare al cinema' = go to the cinema.
From Greek 'bibliothḗkē' (book case). The place to borrow books; 'libreria' is a bookshop.
From 'quarto' (quarter), like the English 'quarter' of a town. 'Quartiere' can also be a military quarters.
Greek 'sêma' (sign) + '-foro' (carrying). 'Al semaforo gira a destra' = turn right at the lights.
Latin 'fontana'. Rome's street drinking fountains are called 'nasoni' (big noses) for their curved spouts.
Latin 'communis'. The 'comune' is Italy's basic unit of local government (nearly 8,000 of them) and also the town-hall building.
From Latin 'aedicula' (little shrine), after the kiosk's shape. Feminine. Sells newspapers, magazines and often bus tickets.
Latin 'insula'. Feminine. 'Isola pedonale' = pedestrian zone. Sicily and Sardinia are 'le isole maggiori'.
From Greek 'periphéreia'. 'In periferia' = on the outskirts. Stress on the 'i': 'pe-ri-fe-REE-a'.
'Lo' before 'st'; plural 'gli stadi'. From Greek 'stádion', originally a unit of length. 'Allo stadio' = at the stadium.
